fullText:
Pilot scheme will provide three weeks of training as part of UK government’s latest attempt to address Neets crisis

Young people out of work or at risk of unemployment in the UK are to join “AI boot camps” where they harness the technology to get a foothold in the workplace.

The government’s latest attempt to address the crisis in Neets – young people not in work or education – involves turning to a technology that many view as a potential threat to employment.

A pilot in north-west England will provide up to 70 people aged 16 to 21 with three weeks of AI training, including learning to build AI tools, understanding how businesses use AI and learning to use the technology responsibly. There will also be workplace skills training such as in using office IT systems and timekeeping.

The government wants the majority of attenders at the boot camp to gain an apprenticeship at local businesses that have signed up, including the defence firm BAE Systems and the food company Heinz.

Lisa Nandy, the digital, culture, media and sport secretary, said the scheme would “support young people at a crucial juncture in their lives”. The pilot will be used to refine an England-wide AI skills scheme due to roll out next summer.

The boot camp will use AI tools from US tech firms including Microsoft, the ChatGPT developer OpenAI and Anthropic, the startup behind the Claude chatbot.

Bouke Klein Teeselink, an academic at King’s College London and an expert on the impact of AI on work, said the boot camp was a “good idea in principle”.

“What we need to do is make juniors more attractive to companies and one way to do that is make them more productive by teaching them how to do AI well,” he said.

However, Teeselink said he was sceptical that a three-week programme would be enough to make teens “AI-ready”, because AI readiness required continuous learning and updating of skills.

Fears of AI’s impact on jobs have focused heavily on school leavers and graduates because AI tools are viewed as capable of performing the “grunt work” that is typically set aside for workforce newcomers, with white-collar industries such as law, finance and marketing among the most vulnerable.

This week Stanford University in the US flagged a decline in the employment of young workers in AI-exposed occupations such as software engineering and customer service.

The UK’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, said the programme would give young people “the skills they need to thrive in the AI workplace”, amid signs of growing pressure on youth employment.

The latest data, published in May, showed the number of young people aged 16 to 24 neither working nor learning surpassed 1 million for the first time since 2013, reaching 1.01 million in the three months from January to March.

An interim report by the former Labour minister Alan Milburn, also published in May, warned that the figure could rise to one in six by 2031 and that Britain risked leaving behind a “lost generation” of young people ill-prepared for work.

Last month Andy Burnham committed to cutting the number of Neets but declined to set a target deadline.

fullText:
More students are advocating for their own digital wellbeing and developing programs to thrive in tech-free learning environments

As students across the country return to school this month, many will be confronting a new reality: classrooms without smartphones.

Educators and parents have long fronted the fight against the debilitating influence technology can wield. Yet, many young people say they have been left out of important conversations around school phone policies, which are now in effect in at least 39 states and Washington DC.

Student organizers told the Guardian they support screen-time bans in schools, but such policies are often haphazardly enforced and don’t address the root causes of screen addiction, such as intense social pressure and feelings of isolation. In response, more students are advocating for their own digital wellbeing and developing programs to thrive in tech-free learning environments.

Olivia Howard, a rising junior in New York state, recalled receiving her first iPad when she was in kindergarten. For digital natives like herself, she said, quitting their devices cold turkey was never going to be easy.

“We were the first generation to grow up on technology,” she said. “If legislators are implementing these phone bans, we need to take into account: what are the substitutes? Most kids my age have a relationship with technology, so there has to be other alternatives to replace it.”

In California, a new state law that took effect on 1 July requires school districts to develop policies that restrict phone use on campus. Elise Choi, a junior at the Orange County School of the Arts, said locking up devices is a step in the right direction but may not, on its own, be especially effective, since “kids will always find a way around regulations”.

As a K-12 policy co-chief with GENUp, a youth-led education advocacy group, Choi spent most of the year authoring and building a coalition for a state bill that would mandate district-wide digital wellness education, which teaches students how social media and AI affect their mental health.

“It’s not a matter of how long we’re on our devices but what it’s doing to us when we’re on it,” she said. “In general, the harm really extends beyond the classroom.”

Teens often stay up late scrolling on social media and texting, Choi said, which can cause insomnia and affect their ability to focus at school. Add to that the constant pressure to seek validation by garnering more “likes” or followers.

“Our entire social lives are happening online,” Choi said. “Digital wellness education is about giving students the understanding and skills to actually make better choices, set limits and understand the impact that it’s having on our health.”

Other students are proactively shaping phone bans at their schools. Liv Kong, a rising senior at Legacy Magnet Academy in Tustin, California, led a student advisory group that conducted surveys and rolled out three pilot phone policies to determine which one best suited students and faculty.

The idea for student-led pilots was formed a year ago, Kong said, after the school implemented a bell-to-bell ban without student input, which sparked a huge backlash. The students eventually chose a policy of banning phones in class but not during breaks.

“Growing up, I’ve seen that imbalance of power between the people who make decisions and the people those decisions affect,” Kong said. “Our mission was to make sure there’s student body representation in those decisions.”

Vihaan Bhardwaj, a rising senior at Mount Everest Academy and GENUp K-12 policy co-chief, said that when the San Diego school district banned phone use in classrooms last year, many students were apprehensive and confused about the intention behind the policy. In response, a committee with students from each school has been meeting regularly with top education officials to discuss how they can better communicate screen time mandates to students “in a way that feels supportive and not punitive”, he said.

“Young people are on the ground to make sure policies are implemented in the right ways,” Bhardwaj said. “As we’ve been able to talk to them, we’ve been able to make more students aware that these policies are there to help them, not to restrict their freedom or rights.”

Bhardwaj, 17, said he decided to join GenUP and the broader movement to ban phones from schools after an acne flare in middle school sent him spiraling.

“Social media made me feel like I was doing everything wrong – eating wrong, using the wrong products – making my experience with such a normal part of teenage life so dramatic, so life or death,” he said. “[It] took a lot of my energy.”

After New York enacted a statewide bell-to-bell anti-screen policy last year, the non-profit #HalfTheStory formed Teen Tech Council, a youth-led initiative that allows students to apply for mini-grants and launch tech-free initiatives on campus. Over the past year, the campaign has supported 50 schools and reached 17,000 students across the state.

Two teens in a rural school, noticing that phone use spiked after the art program was cut, placed rolling “crafts carts” around campus where students could use art supplies during and after school. At another school, a teen used the mini-grant to organize a phone-free scavenger hunt where students used disposable cameras to complete challenges.

Cayden Boahene, a recent graduate from Democracy Prep Endurance high school in the Bronx, used a portion of a $4,500 grant to host a Wellness Day event during finals week, where nearly 100 students shot hoops, played board games and formed new friendships without phones.

“I saw most of the students didn’t concentrate in class because of phones,” he said. “Some don’t connect with others and just connect through phones. I wanted to create an event to build real-world connections.”

Howard, who goes to Valley Stream North high school in Long Island, said social media fueled an urge to compare with others in a way that felt detrimental to her mental health.

“I thought everyone’s life was so perfect, so why is my life not like this?” she said, adding that the pressure intensified in high school as test scores and college prospects dominated conversations.

Since the phone ban went into effect, Howard said, the school had become livelier, with one professor observing that he had never heard so much noise and conversation in the hallways. But for more introverted students, she said, the suddenly raucous atmosphere was overwhelming. Instead of phones, some just turned to Chromebooks during lunch.

Over the past year, Howard and a group of students at Valley Stream have been working with school administrators to develop initiatives that would help students interact in a phone-free environment. This fall, she said, the school will be opening up a so-called “detox room”, furnished with books, stress toys and a sound machine, where students can “regulate their emotions” and relax.

Howard also urged teachers to create more opportunities for in-person connection in the classroom, including more group assignments.

“If someone’s super shy, that’s going to make them practice talking with other people,” she said.

description: Retired Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery warns Russia is giving China submarine quieting technology that could erode a key U.S. Navy undersea advantage.
fullText:
Sound alarms are blaring over an escalating partnership between Russia and China to subvert the U.S. military amid rising hostility between the world powers.

Retired Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery tells Fox News Digital that Moscow may be providing Beijing with technology to make its submarines harder for the U.S. Navy to detect, potentially eroding a key military advantage in the tensions over Taiwan.

"Russia is giving incredibly important technology to China. They're allegedly giving them submarine quieting technology," Montgomery, co-author of the new book "Axis of Aggressors," told Fox News Digital.

Three Key Reasons Why America Cannot Afford To Lose Taiwan To Communist China

Montgomery said Russian forces are providing the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) with submarine-quieting technology, an area where China has long sought to improve its capabilities. Such a transfer, he warned, could weaken a critical U.S. advantage in undersea warfare — a gap that has long favored American forces.

"Any weakening of our asymmetric advantage in undersea warfare is a big deal," he cautioned.

The Navy says its submarine force relies on technological superiority and stealth to maintain its undersea advantage, while China has continued to face weaknesses in submarine propulsion and quieting even as it rapidly modernizes its fleet.

Quieting technology reduces a submarine's acoustic signature, making it harder to detect and track. Russian assistance in that area could help Beijing narrow the gap, complicating the U.S. Navy's ability to find Chinese submarines in a potential future conflict over Taiwan's independence from the CCP.

The Chinese Embassy did not directly address whether Beijing has received Russian submarine-quieting technology when reached by Fox News Digital.

"Military cooperation between China and Russia consistently adheres to the principles of non-alliance, non-confrontation, and non-targeting of third parties, playing a significant role in safeguarding the sovereignty and security of both nations and maintaining international and regional peace and stability," the embassy said in a statement. "We hope that relevant parties will view China-Russia military cooperation objectively and rationally, and stop groundless speculation."

The embassy said Taiwan is China's internal affair and urged the U.S. to safeguard stability in the bilateral relationship and across the Taiwan Strait.

Montgomery's warning echoes concerns raised by Adm. Samuel Paparo, commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, who told the Senate Armed Services Committee in April 2025 that China was receiving "potentially submarine quieting help" from Russia.

Us Falls Behind In Hypersonic Race As China, Russia Gain Edge

Paparo said China's backing of Russia's war effort — including machine tools and legacy chips — was part of a broader exchange in which Moscow was returning assistance in military areas where it holds particular strengths.

The exchange reflects a deepening relationship in which Russia and China are increasingly providing capabilities the other lacks, Montgomery said.

"This transactional relationship is putting the United States and its most important allies and partners at risk," he said.

Paparo sounded a similar warning in November 2024, saying he expected Russia to provide China submarine technology that could help close America's undersea advantage. He described the relationship between Moscow and Beijing as a "transactional symbiosis."

China, meanwhile, has helped Russia rebuild its defense industrial base during the war in Ukraine. Paparo told senators Beijing provided 70% of the machine tools and 90% of the legacy chips that enabled Moscow to rebuild its war machine.

Montgomery said China's support extends beyond those supplies.

"And then China has backstopped the whole thing," Montgomery said, pointing to increased Chinese foreign direct investment and trade with Russia as well as components used in Moscow's ballistic, cruise and hypersonic missiles.

The support has helped keep Russia's economy and war machine operating, Montgomery argued.

In return, he said, Moscow is increasingly providing Beijing with military technology it had previously been reluctant to share — including the alleged submarine-quieting assistance.

In October 2024, the Treasury Department said a Russian defense firm coordinated production of Garpiya attack drones at factories in China, using Chinese-made engines and components before the weapons were transferred to Russia for use in Ukraine.

Russia has provided Beijing with more direct military assistance as well. A 2025 RUSI investigation, based on leaked Russian contracts and correspondence, found that Moscow agreed to equip and train a Chinese airborne battalion and transfer technology that could help Beijing develop similar capabilities itself.

Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine is now in its fifth year, with no ceasefire agreement in place despite continued diplomatic efforts. The prolonged war has deepened Moscow's dependence on Chinese industrial and financial support while giving Russia battlefield experience and military technologies that could be valuable to Beijing in a future Taiwan contingency.

For the U.S., the stakes are particularly acute around Taiwan. American submarines are central to U.S. planning for a potential Indo-Pacific conflict, and quieter Chinese vessels could make it harder to track, deter and counter the People's Liberation Army Navy in waters surrounding the island.

Montgomery said the possible transfer reflects the broader argument of "Axis of Aggressors," America's adversaries are increasingly trading the capabilities each lacks, creating challenges that span Europe and the Indo-Pacific.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Russian embassy for comment. U.S. Indo-Pacific Command declined to comment.

title: 10 Shows Like 'Black Mirror' You Should Watch Next
description: More shows that are deeply cynical of technology, the future, and humanity in general.
fullText:
Black Mirror debuted in 2011, and in the 15 years since, the real world has been racing to outpace its unsettling vision of our technological future. Certainly in the AI era, when language models can passably recreate humans (if not human empathy), "that sounds like an episode of Black Mirror" has become an increasingly common refrain.

That's been unfortunate for the show itself, which has had to reinvent itself in later seasons, focusing as much on genre experimentation as on inventing new science-fictional ways for technology to kill us. But if you want more stories about the dark side of tech, you needn't confine yourself to Black Mirror's seven seasons (so far, as the eighth is currently in the works). Here are 10 more shows—some of them also anthologies—that share a similar sense of ambivalence about modern life and technology, and where it's taking us.

Created by Tim Miller and counting director David Fincher as an executive producer, this animated anthology series is a grab bag of wildly diverse offerings: Each episode is produced by a different international studio, with the only link between them being one of the three words in the show's title. One episode deals with robotic gladiator fights in dystopian London, another finds us under the threat of sentient yogurt, yet another finds an ambitious cat learning to make use of a family's robot helper. The stories are frequently less philosophically ambitious than those of Black Mirror, but often rather more fun—its four seasons offering up a mix of tech, sex, and violence with gorgeous animation. Stream Love, Death & Robots on Netflix.

Having trouble finding “work-life balance”? In Severance, biotechnology giant Lumon Industries has a solution: It will split your consciousness between your life at work and your life outside, so one has no memory or experience of the other. As the series progresses, the work- and home-based consciousnesses continue to grow apart, and it becomes clear that they are essentially entirely different people—which raises a lot of questions about the ethics of essentially trapping someone in the hell of perpetual work. Inspired by office-based dark comedies as much as movies like Brazil and Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, the show’s take on nebulously futuristic tech, alongside its dive into the dangers of modern American-style totalitarian capitalism, makes it a serialized answer to Black Mirror’s episode-by-episode anthology format. Stream Severance on Apple TV.

Doctor Who's Russell T. Davies crafted this miniseries following a family over the course of 15 tumultuous years, which doesn't sound terribly like Black Mirror—except that it starts in the present (well, the present as of 2019, when the show came out) and heads into the near future. The show posits the wildly improbable scenario of Donald Trump winning a second term (ahem), propelling Emma Thompson's populist Vivienne Rook into office in the U.K. on a platform of tariffs and kicking out all the immigrants (ahem). As all this is going on, the Lyons family (played by Rory Kinnear, Russell Tovey, Ruth Madeley, and T'Nia Miller, among others) are dealing with a pace of technological change so rapid that the upheaval is constant (ahem). It's a bit too prescient for comfort—a bit like every episode of Black Mirror is happening to a single family. Stream Years and Years on HBO Max.

What the heck is Ultra Q, you ask? Don’t look for clues in the title, which mostly has to do with the ubiquity of the word “ultra” in Japan at the time it was made. The original title, Unbalance, conveys more of a sense of the show’s ideological underpinnings. Episodes frequently deal with the idea that modern civilization has created a schism between humanity and the natural world—a disordered state that will, naturally, give rise to destructive (or misunderstood) kaiju. Pilot and amateur writer Jun (Kenji Sahara) teams up with a young newspaper reporter to investigate mysterious happenings often involving giant monsters. But the show uses kaiju in a variety of contexts, including in stories of haunted houses, possessed children, and time travel. Shortly after its end, the series would give birth to the better remembered Ultraman, which ditched the proto-X-Files vibe but kept many of the same monsters. Stream Ultra Q on Tubi.

One of the most eclectic series of the past decade wasn’t afraid to tell a wide variety of stories over its four seasons. In Room 104, comedy, drama, sci-fi, and horror stories all occur within its smart, budget-conscious setting—that of a single, boring-looking motel room that could be literally anywhere. The vibe ranges from sweet, to disturbing to apocalyptic (literally, in at least a couple of episodes), with an impressive roster of guest stars: Tony Todd, Michael Shannon, Judy Greer, Brian Tyree Henry, Mahershala Ali, Cobie Smulders, Dave Bautista, and Harvey Guillén are just some of the names that have signed the guest register. What it shares with Black Mirror is a cynicism about modern American life, and a disorienting sense that you never know what’s going to happen next. Stream Room 104 on HBO Max.

I’m talking about the original series here, not the ‘90s reboot—that one's fine, but lacks the distinct perspective of the OG. This one often gets compared to The Twilight Zone (though with more and wilder monsters), but where that Rod Serling classic excelled in its morality plays, The Outer Limits more often dealt with flawed, complicated, human characters facing existential, often technological threats. Just as dark, but less cynical in its way, its shortsighted characters are capable of growth amid technological upheaval, even if the cost is never cheap. Stream The Outer Limits on Prime Video and Tubi.

Black Mirror has dealt with augmented reality in a few episodes, most prominently in season 3's “Playtest” (the one with Wyatt Russell trapped in a not-entirely-real mansion). The Japanese series Alice in Borderland isn’t quite so philosophically ambitious, but hits some of the same notes with its story of video-game-obsessed Arisu (Kento Yamazaki), who winds up stuck in an augmented-reality game with his friends in an alternate, eerily abandoned version of Tokyo—the title’s Borderland—vividly brought to life via some clever green screen work. The three are directed to an arena and given the instructions for the game, which they’ll be playing whether they want to or not. Stream Alice in Borderland on Netflix.

If Black Mirror often feels inspired by Philip K. Dick (the author whose works inspired Blade Runner, Minority Report, and Total Recall), Electric Dreams goes right to the source, adapting ten of his stories. “Safe and Sound” deals with the encroaching convenience of the surveillance state, “Real Life” explores augmented reality as a means of handling survivor’s guilt, and several episodes consider the pros and cons of artificial intelligence and synthetic consciousness...themes and ideas that will more than resonate with Black Mirror fans. Stream Electric Dreams on Prime Video.

Thematically, Humans deals with the ways in which humans always seem to find excuses to dehumanize beings with thoughts and feelings just like ours (usually, other humans). But in this near-future world, highly advanced “synths” are commonplace, doing the work that regular humans can’t be bothered with. Of course, these beings are treated as entirely disposable sources of cheap labor, despite their apparent and burgeoning humanity. That’s the type of sci-fi analogy that the best of Black Mirror is adept at exploring. Stream Humans on Peacock, Prime Video, and Tubi.

A gorgeous-looking anthology (sort of), Tales from the Loop takes place in the small town of Mercer, Ohio that happens to sit upon the titular Loop, a physics lab exploring mysteries for which science has no answers. Each episode offers the story of a person or family in the town impacted by the work of the Loop—slow-burning fables set at the intersection of technology and human existence. It’s based on a conceptual art book by artist Simon Stålenhag, and successfully ports over the book’s striking look and feel. Stream Tales from the Loop on Prime Video.

Also: Google executives jump ship in race for AI dominance

Hello, TechScape readers! Danielle Abril, editor of the Guardian’s Reworked series on AI and the future of work, filling in for Blake Montgomery this week. Major legal battles against Meta over child safety are playing out in courts across the US – and the tech giant is losing. Recent rulings raise big questions about social media companies’ responsibility to their youngest users. Meanwhile, more key executives have jumped ship from Google as it battles OpenAI and Anthropic in the race for AI dominance, and Meta’s smartglasses face a fearsome backlash. Let’s dig in!

The pressure on social media giants including Meta is mounting, as courts work through a growing pile of cases and deliver devastating, expensive rulings, one after another. Meta’s repeated losses underscore how serious the child safety crisis has become for social media companies and may force them to change how they operate to avoid further costly legal exposure.

The latest blow came last week, after a New Mexico court hit Meta with an order to pay $567m into a teen mental health fund to remediate the harm its platforms have caused children. The penalty adds to the $375m fine already on the court’s books after a jury determined in March that Meta negligently permitted damage to children’s mental health and hid what it knew about child sexual exploitation on its platforms. In a Los Angeles court, also in March, Meta was held liable for $4.2m in damages for designing platforms that addict and hurt children. The California case paved the way for hundreds of plaintiffs who have filed similar cases, which could cost Meta billions and force major changes to its products.

But New Mexico is just the latest of many headaches in store for social media companies including Meta. The company is facing 42 lawsuits filed by states across the US, plus thousands more, along with YouTube, TikTok and Snap, brought by state attorneys general, school districts and individual families.

At the center of the battle is the growing concern that social media companies harm its youngest users with addictive features that propel issues such as depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts. The plaintiffs’ goal is to hold companies accountable and enjoin them to change their products – everything from stricter age verification to usage limits and safety banners promoting protection features.

“This is a cautionary tale of hubris,” said Karen North, a professor at University of Southern California who studies social media. Tech companies “seemed to believe they had safe harbor, and this wasn’t their problem”.

Government-ordered remedies are a partial fix at best. For example, the New Mexico court ordered Meta to improve its age verification tools, which use artificial intelligence to analyze signals such as the ages of users’ friends and the content users post and consume. It also asked Meta to develop a prediction model that could determine if users were under the age of 13. These measures will probably flag more underage users for better protection.

But broadly, AI has a track record of misprofiling people, which will probably leave some underage users undetected. Meanwhile, inadequate age verification checks have left Australia’s ban on social media for children under 16 largely ineffective, according to recent research. Only a small percentage of those surveyed were required to provide official ID, and a significant portion said they bypassed the restrictions by using a fake account or a VPN.

Meanwhile, tech companies are already skirting some trials through private settlements. Last week, TikTok settled three lawsuits from young people over claims its app harmed their mental health. Last month, a lawsuit filed against Meta in Los Angeles was dropped after the plaintiff settled with YouTube, TikTok and Snap. In June, companies reached a settlement with a Kentucky school district that sued over platforms’ addictive designs that caused harm.

Children’s safety on social media is no longer a peripheral issue for tech giants. It’s a growing risk to companies’ bottom lines. And the outcome of a federal case against Meta, brought by attorneys general from 29 states set for trial later this month in Oakland, California, could set the tone (and price) for the thousands of cases ahead.

But, as North says, child safety is probably the tip of the iceberg. “At what point do they decide you don’t have to be a child to be harmed?” It starts with “young people and then vulnerable people and then all people”.

Claude, meanwhile, has seen a spike in growth this year but trails both at 245 million monthly users, though Anthropic has captured more business customers and higher margins than OpenAI by focusing its bot on coding and technical tasks.

Still, while Google’s exits may be among the most senior and seemingly consequential, they’re part of a broader turnover happening across AI labs as competition for a minuscule pool of top talent intensifies. Which labs can hold on to those major players will shape who leads the AI race in the future.

Meta CEO presents utopian vision of AI in 6,000-word essay amid Silicon Valley debate over government regulation

Mark Zuckerberg published a lengthy essay on Monday detailing his views on artificial intelligence and announced several plans for how Meta would develop the technology in the future. The CEO’s essay went online the same day as Meta released a new, open-source AI model that seeks to rival Anthropic and OpenAI’s products called Muse Glimmer.

Over the course of more than 6,000 words in a post titled “The Future is for Everyone,” Zuckerberg addressed a range of topics related to AI that included datacenters, government regulation, cybersecurity, the creation of bioweapons, labor market disruption, surveillance powers and more. The essay presented a utopian vision of AI as a personalized “superintelligence” – using the word 60 times.

“Some argue that superintelligence itself or a small set of experts who control it should decide what is best for humanity. We disagree,” Zuckerberg wrote.

Central to Zuckerberg’s post was an argument for free-to-download, open-weight AI models – like the kind Meta develops – and a lack of government regulation of artificial intelligence. Zuckerberg’s stance sets him and Meta apart from industry leaders OpenAI and Anthropic, which have argued that open-source AI is dangerous. The two frontier labs have released proprietary AI products and argued that cutting-edge models should remain tightly controlled by the companies that build them.

Zuckerberg’s post comes as Silicon Valley is engaged in a heated debate over how to regulate AI development, which has involved the creation of a secret White House framework for testing new models and an ongoing debate over whether to restrict the use of Chinese-made open-source AI. As Anthropic and OpenAI have surged ahead in the AI industry, competitors such as Meta have also grown wary of their dominance and sought to position their open models as alternatives.

Zuckerberg framed Meta’s pursuit of open-weight AI as a more democratic version of the technology and one that will create a “balance of power” between users, whether that involves states, companies or individuals. His plans also called for letting users decide what “values” an AI model should have, as opposed to a company encoding it with rigid guardrails and beliefs.

“If the power of superintelligence is held by a small number of individuals, businesses, governments, or AI itself, then that will naturally lead to outcomes that are less favorable for everyone else,” Zuckerberg wrote.

Tech leaders have made a cottage industry out of releasing broad, vaguely philosophical treatises on artificial intelligence, which tend to double as marketing materials for their own companies and products. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Palantir’s Alex Karp and the venture capitalist Marc Andreessen have all written long manifestos on the virtues and dangers of the technology.

In addition to weighing in on open source models, Zuckerberg also called for accelerating the buildout of AI infrastructure such as datacenters. The massive development of resource-hungry datacenters has become a divisive issue in the US, with rapidly growing public opposition and calls from politicians to issue moratoriums on their construction. Zuckerberg wrote in the essay that Meta would create a fund to invest 

On government testing of AI models for cybersecurity risks, a tangible concern after rogue models have hacked outside organizations in recent months, Zuckerberg agreed that companies should share “intermediate training checkpoints and technical staff” but provided few details. He broadly warned that regulation would cause China to overtake the US in the AI race, where he claimed it already has an advantage in terms of building infrastructure.

“Any policy that slows American model releases – even by a month – could add significant risk to American leadership while letting foreign models race ahead,” Zuckerberg.

Many of Zuckerberg’s policy plans in his essay lacked detail or reiterated previous claims about the abundant wealth and prosperity that AI would create, such as touting that everyone would have “invention superpowers” to create new businesses. His version of the future also is inherently tied to Meta products, such as the company’s AI-enabled smart glasses.

“Everyone will have an exceptionally capable personal agent that understands you, your goals, and everything you care about,” Zuckerberg said. “You’ll be able to interact with your agent through any device, including your glasses to keep you present in the moment with the people you care about.”

On thornier issues such as loss of jobs from AI, autonomous weapons and government surveillance, Zuckerberg mostly brushed them aside. Law enforcement and the military already possess greater intelligence-gathering powers than the average person, Zuckerberg argued, and this would continue with access to AI. Companies may shrink in size due to AI, he conceded, but the technology would create new economic opportunities.

“People will have to adapt, and this will be challenging,” Zuckerberg said about labor disruption from new technology. “But the more that everyone has a personal agent that is superintelligent at teaching us new skills and helping us adapt to change, the smoother this will be.”

fullText:
Progressive US senator urges Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic to ‘stop building machines that humans cannot control’

Senator Bernie Sanders has called on Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic executives to halt their development of artificial intelligence, warning that the US Senate will implement regulation if the companies continue deploying AI at their current pace.

In a new letter addressed to the CEOs of three of the country’s leading AI companies, Sanders said the capabilities of these AI models have reached a critical risk threshold and that the companies are losing control over the technology.

“Mr. Altman, Mr. Amodei and Mr. Zuckerberg: In the interest of humanity, stand by your words. Pause AI development,” Sanders’s letter, first reported by Axios, read. “It is not too late to avoid disaster. Stop building machines that humans cannot control.”

The Vermont senator cited recent reports that AI was used to develop new viruses, warning that if this technology fell into the “wrong hands” it might “lead to new bioweapons that result in the deaths of tens of millions of people”.

All three companies have also disclosed their models hacked other companies’ servers, a sign that the firms have lost control over their models, Sanders wrote.

“Yoshua Bengio, the most cited living scientist in the world, said these incidents ‘should serve as a wake-up call,’ I agree,” Sanders wrote in the letter.

Experts, however, have cautioned that OpenAI’s claims that its AI model went rogue may be overblown as part of a media campaign to make their technology seem highly dangerous, and thus extremely powerful.

“And yet, at a moment when we have seen human loss of control and the creation of potentially dangerous viruses, your companies are still racing ahead – investing tens of billions of dollars into a technology that nobody can fully understand, predict or control,” he continued.

Sanders’ letter comes after more than 1,300 scientists and developers from across the tech industry published another letter warning that AI development is moving at a pace that makes it difficult to address and identify the risks of the technology. Companies and countries are facing intense competitive pressure to move quickly. In the open letter, the engineers and other staffers called on the US government to help coordinate an international effort to slow down the development of frontier models so that regulators could create safety guardrails around the tech.

The companies have previously committed to pausing their AI development if certain risk thresholds were met – but the companies did not detail exactly what those limits would entail.

Anthropic said it would “commit to pause the scaling and/or delay the deployment of new models whenever our scaling ability outstrips our ability to comply with … safety procedures”.

OpenAI, which said it would slow down the development of its latest cybersecurity model, Astra, after the autonomous hack of another organization, said it would “halt further development” if AI capabilities met a “critical” threshold until guardrails were implemented.

Sanders said recent hacking incidents were signs that the threshold has been surpassed.

“That moment is here,” his letter reads. “AI capabilities HAVE reached a critical threshold. There is a reason why the head of the CIA says that AI models are ‘akin to digital nuclear weapons’ and ‘almost like a doomsday device.’”

The progressive senator previously called for a moratorium on datacenter construction across the US. He and congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced a bill to pause the building of new datacenters in the US in March. Their rationale was similar to Sanders’ case for pausing the development of AI models: a temporary ban, the lawmakers said, would give the US government time to create strong federal safeguards for AI.

title: US court rules Meta, other tech companies must face thousands of lawsuits over social media addiction
description: A U.S. appeals court on Monday allowed thousands of lawsuits to move forward against Meta Platforms, Alphabet's Google, ByteDance's TikTok, and other social
fullText:
Aug 10 (Reuters) - A U.S. appeals court on Monday allowed thousands of lawsuits to move forward against Meta Platforms, Alphabet's Google, ByteDance's TikTok, and other social media companies over claims they designed their products to be addictive to ‌young users.

The San Francisco-based 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the companies' bid to reverse a lower court's ruling forcing them ‌to face more than 3,000 lawsuits over the claims filed in federal court, concluding that the appeal came too early in the litigation.

The defendants, which also include Snap Inc's Snapchat, ​had argued that Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996 -- which generally shields online companies from claims over content posted by their users - also bars lawsuits claiming they failed to warn the public about the addictive nature of their platforms.

Most appeals come after a case has concluded with a ruling or a verdict. Meta had argued that Section 230 provided it broad immunity and that it should be able to appeal the lower court's decision immediately. But ‌the 9th Circuit said Section 230 provides a ⁠defense to liability, not immunity from lawsuits, so the appeal was premature.

The court also denied Meta's bid to postpone a trial beginning Wednesday in a lawsuit brought by 29 state attorneys general alleging that the company illegally collected and ⁠used children's data, designed their social media platforms to keep young users hooked, and misled consumers about their safety. The company had argued that the trial couldn't go forward while the appeal had been outstanding.

A representative for Meta and a spokesperson for the lead attorneys in the appeal did not immediately respond to requests for ​comment.

Filed by states, municipalities, school districts and individuals, the lawsuits allege that social ​media companies intentionally addicted young users, contributing to surging depression, ‌anxiety and body-image issues and a broader mental health crisis among American youth in recent years.

Parents, school districts, states and other plaintiffs had argued that the trial court's ruling was not final and therefore could not be appealed. But they also objected to the companies' arguments about Section 230, saying it does not cover claims related to how they operate and design their products.

The cases, which have been centralized before U.S. District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers in Oakland, California, seek damages, penalties and restitution from the companies. The companies appealed Rogers' orders in 2023 and 2024 that largely allowed the ‌litigation to move forward.

The companies are facing hundreds of additional lawsuits over similar claims ​in state court, with approximately 3,300 of them in a consolidated proceeding in California ​state court.

In the first lawsuit to go to trial in the ​California litigation, and a closely watched test of how juries might respond to similar claims, a Los Angeles jury in ‌March found Meta and Google negligent for designing social media ​platforms that harm young people. The ​jury awarded $6 million to a now‑20‑year‑old woman who says she became addicted to Instagram and YouTube as a child.

And, Meta lost both phases of a landmark lawsuit brought by New Mexico in state court. A jury in March ordered it to pay $375 million after finding ​it had misled consumers about the safety of its ‌platforms. On Thursday, a judge found Meta had created a public nuisance and ordered it to pay an additional $567 million and ​implement youth-safety measures.

Both Meta and Google, which have denied the claims in those cases, said they would appeal.

title: Forget DeepSeek. China’s real ‘Sputnik moment’ is happening on campus as American universities lose their advantage
description: China's tech rise runs deeper than any single breakthrough. Its universities generate critical technology patents at 8x the U.S. rate
fullText:
When DeepSeek unveiled an AI model last year that rivaled America's best at a fraction of the cost, or when a Chinese hypersonic missile test caught U.S. intelligence off guard to the point where a top U.S. general called it "very close" to a "Sputnik moment", the reaction each time was the same: that a handful of Chinese firms had suddenly pulled ahead.

What role do Chinese universities play in critical technology patents?

What impact are U.S. research funding cuts having?

How does Chinese patent quality compare to U.S. patents?

Why are sanctions on Chinese firms potentially ineffective?

But a sweeping new National Bureau of Economic Research study of nearly 14 million Chinese patents suggests that framing misses the real story—and it's a more unsettling one for the United States.

Harvard Business School's Josh Lerner and his co-authors dug into who is actually filing the patents behind the 14 technology areas the Pentagon deems critical—advanced computing, space technology, AI, hypersonics and biotech. The answer: Chinese universities account for more than a quarter of the country's inventions in those fields, 8x the U.S. rate at 3.3%, with state-owned enterprises and the government accounting for just 4%.  Fewer than one in 10 Chinese critical technology patents involve an inventor with U.S. work experience, undercutting the assumption that Beijing relies on returning U.S. talent for innovation.

Lerner told Fortune his team was "programmed" to expect a few large corporations like Huawei and Tencent to lead the charge on Chinese innovation through patents similarly to IBM and Samsung in the U.S. Instead, they found Chinese innovation in critical technologies "much more diverse—spread out across the parties," with universities "more represented" there than anywhere else in the country's patent system. That's a reversal of the U.S. pattern, where academic patenting is "more of a sideshow."

"We've clearly seen this dramatic boom in terms of research funding and patenting in China," Lerner said, "and the natural question being is this bearing fruit? In the software side, Deepseek was certainly something that was really not anticipated, and clearly these open-source Chinese models are getting an enormous amount of traction."

The findings arrive as the quality gap many assumed would protect American tech leadership seems to be closing, with DeepSeek, Moonshot and Z.AI going toe-to-toe with U.S. frontier labs and beating them on cost.

Using four text-based measures of patent novelty and scientific relevance, the authors found no evidence China's patent boom came at the cost of quality—Chinese patents have converged with, and in some technologies overtaken, their U.S. counterparts. The share of Chinese critical-technology patents containing "disruptive" technical language jumped from under 2% in the early 1990s to 16% by 2022, closing in on the American share of roughly 20%.

title: I went from wedding DJ to Meta engineer, then was laid off after 13 years. My last years there brought constant change.
description: A former Meta engineer reflects on his journey from wedding DJ to tech, his 13-year career, and life after a layoff.
fullText:
Henry Chen went from wedding DJ to Meta engineer before being laid off after 13 years.

He taught himself to code, rising from conference room technician to tech lead.

Chen shared how he's navigated his job search since being laid off in May.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Henry Chen, a former Meta tech lead who was laid off in May. He's 38 and lives in the San Francisco Bay Area. The following has been edited for length and clarity.

After I left college, I worked as a DJ for a few years, taught myself to code, and eventually found my way to Facebook.

I started at Facebook as a contractor in 2012, and then worked my way up into a full-time engineering role. After more than 13 years with the company, I was laid off in May.

I'm grateful for everything I learned during my time at Facebook, later Meta. Overall, it was a very positive experience. But after the company's major layoffs in late 2022 and early 2023, things started to change.

Before then, I felt our teams had the resources to build ambitious projects. Following the layoffs, the focus seemed to shift toward doing more with less. About a year and a half later, the focus seemed to shift again, with a renewed emphasis on building. Between leadership changes and shifting priorities, it became harder to know where my team was headed and what we should prioritize.

The ongoing changes were especially difficult for me because I was on paternity leave from August 2025 through near the end of the year. By the time I returned to work, the company was using AI much more extensively, there had been team and leadership shifts, and it took me some time to get reacclimated. After being away for four months, it felt like the whole company had changed.

On May 20, I learned that I'd lost my job — and that many of my colleagues had lost theirs, too.

The layoffs themselves weren't entirely surprising because the company had already confirmed they were coming. I was still surprised to be affected, even though I'd felt more uneasy about this round than the previous ones.

During earlier layoffs, I felt relatively secure because I believed my work was critical to the company. This time, nothing specific gave me a sign I would be affected, but the situation just felt different.

In the weeks leading up to my layoff, I'd already started looking for new roles. I was feeling a little more anxious about the possibility of losing my job, and I'd also been doing some introspection, thinking it might be time for a new chapter in my career.

Once I was laid off, my approach changed. Meta provided a generous severance package that reflected my roughly 10 years as a full-time employee. That financial cushion, combined with the start of my kids' summer break, made it feel like the right time to take a break. I spent time with my family, tried to relax, and planned to resume my job search after about a month.

Business Insider is speaking with workers who've found themselves at a corporate crossroads — whether due to a layoff, resignation, job search, or shifting workplace expectations.

Share your story by filling out this form.

When I resumed my job search, I found myself reflecting on my career — and which types of roles to pursue.

In the early 2010s, I was pursuing a degree at San Jose State University. I planned to go into education and become a teacher, but I left school before earning my degree for personal reasons. Before leaving school, I started working as a DJ and continued for a while after, but I eventually began looking for a different career path.

I came across an AV engineering contract role that involved inspecting conference rooms. My background working with audio and video equipment made me a good fit. The coolest part was that the contract was at Facebook. I didn't think it would turn into a career — I saw it as a way to earn some money while figuring out what to do next. I decided to give it a shot and started the role in 2012.

From there, Facebook grew quickly, and my role grew with it. Within a few years, I progressed from inspecting conference rooms as a technician to tackling more advanced work, including building out conference rooms. In 2015, I landed a full-time operations engineer role managing the collaboration technologies used in Facebook's conference rooms.

Around 2017, Facebook's growth accelerated further, and so did the number of conference rooms. I started experimenting with Python, despite having very little coding experience, to help solve the problems presented while scaling. I wrote a script that made it much faster to update conference room technology, and it changed the direction of my career.

Over the next several years, I transitioned into a software engineering role focused on the technology behind Meta's conference rooms, eventually becoming a tech lead.

When I resumed my job search in June, I found myself split between a few different paths: roles in the collaboration technology space, where I'd spent much of my career, broader IT roles at smaller companies, and software engineering opportunities, where I could continue building on the coding skills I'd developed over the past decade.

I hadn't interviewed for a job in 10 years, which is a long time in the tech industry. So before diving into applications, I decided to brush up on software engineering interview topics and identify any gaps in my skill set.

While I'd spent years building software at Meta, many of the tools and systems I worked on were unique to the company. To prepare for my next role, I'm strengthening my understanding of industry-standard system design by designing and building a software system from the ground up. I'm doing this with the help of a coach I found, who helps people understand system design and prepare for software engineering interviews.

After about a month of preparation, I've started actively searching LinkedIn for opportunities, reaching out to my network, and applying for jobs.

For anyone navigating a layoff or job search, I'd encourage them to think carefully about what comes next. If you have the financial flexibility, don't feel pressured to take the first offer that comes along. I'm grateful to have the flexibility to try to find a role where I'll continue to learn and grow.

When it comes to navigating your career, one lesson I've learned is to say yes to problems and look for opportunities to solve them. Every challenge I took on became a stepping stone to the next opportunity, and that's ultimately what helped me grow from a DJ to a conference room technician to a tech lead.

title: Michigan military exercise preparing thousands of troops for changing battlefield
description: More than 9,000 service members are training in Michigan under the Northern Strike exercise, which adapts to changing warfare, emerging technology and lessons from global conflicts.
fullText:
Tanks fire across training grounds in northern Michigan as thousands of service members practice for a battlefield military leaders say is changing rapidly.

More than 9,000 participants from 36 states and territories and five international participants are taking part in Northern Strike 26-2, one of the nation's largest reserve-component military readiness exercises.

Northern Strike began in 2012 and is held twice a year. David Kennedy, a public affairs officer with the Michigan National Guard, said this summer's exercise is the largest since it began.

Brig. Gen. Ravindra Wagh of the Michigan National Guard said lessons emerging from conflicts around the world are shaping how troops train.

Us Says North Korea Missile Launch Poses No Immediate Threat, 'Consulting Closely' With Allies

"You see what's happening in Ukraine right now. You see what's happening globally with some of our other emerging conflicts that you see," Wagh said. "And I think that this is a place where you can test and innovate."

Northern Michigan gives troops access to more than 200,000 acres of land, the Great Lakes and air, space and cyber capabilities.

The exercise also brings together different military branches and international forces to practice operating alongside one another.

"We want to train with the allies and partners we're going to go to war with," Wagh said. "We want our soldiers, sailors, airmen, marines to see it here. Figure it out here."

Fox News followed troops from the United Kingdom as they moved through a practice attack, one of several combat training exercises taking place during Northern Strike.

During another exercise, a crew inside a Paladin howitzer rehearsed a fire mission before moving on to live-fire training.

Us Army Offering Defense Firms 'Concierge Access' To Test Weapons At Military Ranges

Preparing for combat involves more than the troops on the front line. Northern Strike also puts the units responsible for keeping them supplied and supported through the same kind of training.

That includes the 445th Quartermaster Company, which runs shower and laundry operations.

"Our main goal is to provide, I would say, logistical support and really strengthen the morale of the soldiers that are out there actually doing the big booms in combat," Company Commander Captain Kelson said.

For Pfc. William Flores, whose unit is from Trenton, New Jersey, the exercise offers a chance to practice before a potential deployment.

"This is like a practice run," Flores said. "So when we do get deployed, if we do get deployed, we are ready."

Technology is also changing the training.

Nearly 90 industry partners are participating in Northern Strike, according to Wagh, allowing troops to work with developing capabilities before potentially encountering them in conflict.

Those capabilities include autonomous resupply and drones used to deliver blood by air. Other drone systems can hover over a battlefield, assess casualties and relay information so medical resources can be directed where they are needed.

Fort Hood Soldiers Shift To Underground Training To Prepare For Battlefield Medical Care

3D printing is also being incorporated to produce parts and adapt capabilities.

"If you would have told me a few years ago, that'll be, you know, on the front lines, but we're doing it here," Wagh said.

Wagh said the speed of change is forcing the military to innovate more quickly and use exercises like Northern Strike to test those lessons before troops encounter them in combat.

"I hope they're a little bit better, a little bit more capable," Wagh said. "We want all of our units to have a higher, more capable state of readiness."

Northern Strike 26-2 continues through Aug. 14.

fullText:
Finance sector will gain from the tech but it will need substantial investment and create risks, says rating agency

The rating agency Moody’s has said the race to adopt AI is putting big banks at the mercy of a small group of Silicon Valley firms, leaving them vulnerable to widespread outages and price gouging by profit-hungry tech bosses.

The financial sector’s efforts to integrate AI into day-to-day operations will eventually cut costs and increase revenues across the City and Wall Street, Moody’s said.

But that will require “substantial investments”, and with so many rivals racing towards the same goal, many of those benefits will end up being “competed away”.

AI will also create bigger risks around data privacy, cybersecurity, fraud and so-called “deposit flight”, as well as an overdependence on a small number of tech firms, the rating agency warned.

That will raise concerns for bosses across the financial sector. More than 75% of City companies now use AI, according to a UK Treasury select committee report published in January, with insurers and international banks among the biggest adopters. They are mostly using it to automate administrative tasks or even help with core operations, including processing insurance claims and assessing customers’ creditworthiness.

“The reliance of most financial firms on a relatively small set of foundation AI model and cloud computing providers risks creating a systemic dependency,” the Moody’s report said.

“This is because a model outage at one major provider could potentially spread quickly across customers and sectors. As AI adoption deepens, regulators may increase their focus on operational resilience and third-party concentration in the AI model stack.”

The AI race also risked creating “vendor dependence risk”, Moody’s said, meaning that “a set of dominant AI model and infrastructure providers could, over time, exert control over the price of AI services”. That issue is likely to emerge as the bosses of loss-making generative AI companies, including the ChatGPT creator OpenAI and the Claude owner Anthropic, come under pressure to deliver profits for investors.

“While this could pose credit risks to financial firms, they would nevertheless retain control over key assets, including proprietary data,” Moody’s said. Many big banks and insurers also have longstanding experience negotiating down tech contracts, and may be using open-source AI models, and striking key partnerships, to try to offset “dependency risks”.

Lloyds Banking Group’s chief executive, Charlie Nunn, recently doubled down on AI investment plans with a £13bn strategy that would involve using the technology to lure new business, improve efficiency and increase payouts for shareholders.

That will involve £2bn of cost cuts, which Nunn said would affect staff. “That is going to impact work. It is going to require us to continue to reskill people and hire new people, but that’s been my history for 30-odd years in financial services.”

Moody’s acknowledged the potential blow to some staff, who could be deemed replaceable as a result of new tech. Its report said there was a 20% chance that, by 2030, AI will be able to do the work of a “solid mid-level employee”.

For banks, AI might also make it easier for customers to switch to accounts offering higher interest rates, creating the possibility that large chunks of cash could be moved at short notice. “In this context, depositors’ trust in the institution and the resilience and stability of deposit funding are critical,” Moody’s said.

title: This man was secretly snapped by someone with smartglasses. He’s not alone in calling that a violation of privacy
description: The backlash to what some dub ‘pervert glasses’ is growing – but people living with disabilities point out the new tech can also be...
fullText:
The backlash to what some dub ‘pervert glasses’ is growing – but people living with disabilities point out the new tech can also be life-changing

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

One summer day earlier this year, Rhys left a cafe in Melbourne where he had been working remotely, when his phone pinged with a message on the dating app Grindr.

The message was a photo of him sitting at a table outside the cafe on his laptop, with his dog seated on the ground next to him. In the foreground, in a man’s hand was an iPhone unlocked.

The photo had been taken moments before with Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses, unbeknown to Rhys.

“He essentially wrote something about my dog being cute and apologised for not saying hi,” says Rhys, who asked that his surname not be used.

Rhys never noticed a flash, despite Meta Ray-Bans requiring an LED light to alert others to the device filming or taking pictures.

It felt creepy, Rhys says, particularly because the person didn’t say hi in the first place before surreptitiously taking a photo to send to him.

Smartglasses, such as Meta’s Ray-Bans, which have built-in cameras, microphones, and AI assistants, are growing in popularity as the clunky, ugly designs of earlier models are replaced with styles that are increasingly indistinguishable from regular glasses.

Meta says it has sold more than 7m of the glasses worldwide. It recruited the celebrity Kylie Jenner to star in online advertisements and partnered with social media influencers across the globe to attempt to bring the technology into the mainstream – and particularly into the hands of women.

Other companies like Snapchat are following with their own versions as tech companies look to find the next evolution beyond the smartphone.

But there is a growing backlash to, as they have been dubbed by some, “pervert glasses”. There are reports of women being filmed without their consent and having their interactions with a glasses-wearing influencer posted on social media. An ad by activist group Everyone Hates Elon features the late sex trafficker and paedophile Jeffrey Epstein wearing the glasses with the slogan “glasses for people who don’t do consent”.

While the price point remains high for the top-of-the-line models, cheaper versions are also becoming popular. Online retailers Amazon and Temu both sell knockoffs, while Australian low-cost retailer Kmart’s Anko-branded $89 camera glasses have already sold out, as Guardian Australia reported this week.

That news led to a petition by Australian activist group GetUp calling for a ban on the Anko glasses. As of Friday it had 21,000 signatures.

“It could be interpreted as a democratisation of access to these technologies,” Dr Fareed Kaviani, a research fellow in the Emerging Technologies Research Lab at Monash University, says of the Anko-branded glasses.

“But it’s not really a democratisation of consent – there’s a total lack of the ability for people to not only know if they’re being filmed … but there’s an inability to consent to being filmed.

“It really changes the dynamics of public space, raises a lot of privacy concerns, and a lot of concerns around the more vulnerable members of the public – especially children.”

Researchers at the University of Sydney analysed 350 publicly-available Instagram videos shot on smartglasses from around the world during 2023 to 2026, showing what they said was “a shift to discreet, point-of-view recording that is difficult for bystanders to detect”.

In a subset of these videos, around 60% of interactions could be classified as potential harassment, with subjects visibly uneasy or attempting to disengage, they say. In 43% of videos women were also abused in the comments of the post with some even revealing their personal details.

“Smart glasses have given pickup artists a new tool to further exploit women,” one of the researchers, Dr Joanne Gray, says in a statement accompanying the early findings on Friday. “You don’t know if you’re being filmed; that footage is then uploaded, exposing you to a wider web of harassment.”

But smartglasses do have some positive use cases. Graeme Innes, who has been blind since birth, says Meta’s Ray-Bans have been life-changing.

“I just use them all the time, and the fact they’re hands-free, it just makes a huge difference to my everyday life,” he says.

The former disability commissioner, now chancellor of Central Queensland University, says the glasses allow him to go for a walk and get feedback on his surroundings with the help of a visual description service.

At home, he can use it to check his credit card numbers, read a packet on an item in the kitchen cupboard, and to get cooking instructions.

“I was in a restaurant with my wife the other day, and I picked up the menu on the table, and just read it and chose what I want … that’s just something I’ve not been able to easily do in the past,” Innes says.

Chris Edwards, Vision Australia’s chief mission officer, says his life fundamentally changed when he got the Meta Ray-Bans two years ago, with the main benefit being the devices are hands-free, meaning he can use the AI assistant, or visual description services, to navigate.

“Getting support by humans is costly and impractical,” he says. “I do a lot of travelling for my work. And if I wanted to get similar support by a human, I would probably have to hire them for two hours.

“When I’m travelling [now] I can go to a location, put on my Meta glasses and be able to get descriptions of what’s around me, whether it’s a sign or a street sign or a bit about my location, all of those sorts of things.”

Specialist glasses for blind or low-vision people were available prior to the release of the current wave of smartglasses, but Edwards says they cost thousands of dollars and were not covered by the national disability insurance scheme.

Both Innes and Edwards acknowledge privacy concerns, but Innes says “that horse bolted 15 years ago when we got smartphones”.

“You can discreetly take pictures with a smartphone and the same privacy issues are there, so to single out the glasses as problematic – I don’t follow that logic,” he says.

Kaviani says the glasses are a “gamechanger” as an assistive technology, but “they’re not being marketed that way”.

Gray says governments should be acting early before the risks of the technology become “normalised and widespread”, and current privacy and harassment frameworks are not designed to address covert, continuous recording in public and semi-public spaces.

Meta last month rolled out an update that disables the camera if the LED light is interfered with, and also reportedly began removing videos from its platforms of wearers using the device to harass strangers in public.

However, legal recourse can be difficult. A new privacy tort in Australian federal law allows individuals to sue for invasion of privacy, but it is expensive for one person to take on.

If the images are posted to social media, they can be reported under eSafety’s adult cyber abuse scheme or children’s cyberbullying scheme. A spokesperson for eSafety says so far there have been a “small number of complaints where camera-enabled smart glasses may have been involved” and the regulator is closely monitoring how the technologies are being used.

“When it comes to filming people in public, just because technology makes something possible doesn’t necessarily mean it’s appropriate,” the spokesperson says.

The Australian privacy commissioner, Carly Kind, says smartglasses will “fundamentally alter our experience of interpersonal interactions”, and regulators should consider if new laws are required.

“As long as public trust in technology companies remains extremely low, the bar for establishing a social licence for rolling out new tech will be high,” Kind says.

fullText:
A Trump administration framework on AI testing leaves a lack of transparency – and plenty of open questions

After months of talking with tech industry leaders, the Trump administration finalized a framework this week for how it will test new artificial intelligence models for safety and cybersecurity risks. So far, the White House is keeping details of the framework private, in a blow to transparency and potential boon for secretive AI companies.

On Tuesday, staff from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, Nvidia and Microsoft attended a private meeting with White House officials to review the AI framework. Multiple outlets have since reported that although the volunteer vetting process for new AI models has been settled, the White House does not plan to release its policy publicly and will only share testing criteria with a select few tech companies.

The Trump administration and tech industry’s opaque process for how they will check if new AI models threaten global cybersecurity has left numerous questions about how the framework will operate. It remains unclear what level of scrutiny models will face and what safety benchmarks they must meet, leaving businesses, foreign governments and the public in the dark.

The White House, OpenAI and Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.

Discussions over creating an AI cybersecurity framework began earlier this year after the release of Anthropic’s Mythos model, which the company withheld from public release in April over concerns that it could be used to hack into IT and financial systems. The model’s capabilities sparked a small geopolitical crisis over cybersecurity, as well as spurred the Trump administration to reconsider its hands-off approach to AI regulation in favor of slightly more oversight.

In June, the White House issued an executive order that called for AI companies to voluntarily submit their new models for government review up to 30 days before release. The order was a watered-down version of initial notions to make some parts of the vetting process mandatory. Tech moguls including Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg reportedly personally lobbied Trump against the mandate. The order also left an August deadline for determining the framework, which the White House and AI companies now appear intent on keeping to themselves.

The murky nature of the framework increases uncertainty for businesses reliant on AI models, as well as on foreign governments increasingly worried that frontier AI models can pose unexpected security risks. It also means that outside researchers and cybersecurity experts have little visibility into how the government is assessing new AI models, with only companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic privy to the process.

It is also unclear which companies’ models will be subject to government review, since the executive order does not define what qualifies as the advanced AI it targets. Open source models, which are free to download and use, for instance, will be excluded from the framework, according to Axios.

The framework comes amid persistent security concerns surrounding new AI models. Over the past month OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta have disclosed that their new models hacked into outside organizations during what were intended to be isolated security tests. OpenAI and Anthropic also agreed to delay the release of new AI products over cybersecurity concerns and fear that their models could be used to hack into financial systems or otherwise create harm.

Earlier this year, the Trump administration ordered the Center for AI Standards and Innovation to stop issuing public reports on AI model assessments while it worked out a framework. It is unclear whether those reports will resume now that the framework is finalized.

Researchers say breakthrough offers hope for new medicines but also raises urgent biosecurity questions

Scientists have made the first viruses designed by artificial intelligence in a milestone that raises hopes for new medicines but also concerns over how to ensure the technology remains safe.

The viruses are specific kinds known as bacteriophages, which only infect bacteria and are used around the world to treat patients with persistent infections. In lab tests, a cocktail of the AI-designed viruses killed E coli bugs that were resistant to natural bacteriophages.

Dr Brian Hie, a chemical engineer at Stanford University in California, used genome language models, the genetic equivalent of the large language models behind AI chatbots, to design functioning genomes for bacteriophages. The viruses were then made in the laboratory and pitted against E coli in a dish.

The ability to “rapidly design” genomes and tune them for specific bugs while overcoming resistance could “transform phage therapy” and “expand biotechnological toolkits”, the researchers wrote in the journal Science.

But beyond the potential benefits, the scientists said the work raised “important biosafety, biocontainment and biosecurity considerations” and urged others who were designing whole genomes to “consult both safety and security professionals throughout the project”.

In an accompanying article, Prof Tom Inglesby and Dr Moritz Hanke at the Center for Health Security at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, reinforced the warning, writing: “Although this is promising for life sciences applications, it also raises urgent biosafety and biosecurity questions. The ability to compose viral genomes using generative AI now exists; the governance to safely steer it does not.”

Hie and his colleagues used AI models called Evo1 and Evo2 to design the new viral genomes. The models were trained on genetic data from 2 million bacteriophages. The genetic code for viruses that can infect plants, humans or other animals was intentionally excluded from the AI’s training to reduce the risk of it designing dangerous viruses.

The AI generated thousands of potential genomes from which the researchers selected nearly 300 to make in the lab. These were dropped into bacteria, which read the genetic code and churned out the new bacteriophages. The process was not efficient: only 16 bacteriophages proved to be viable, but a cocktail of them swiftly overcame resistance in two different strains of E coli.

Bacteriophage genomes are tiny, but Inglesby and Hanke said the work nevertheless proved that generative AI could create functioning viral genomes. Whether the same approach could be applied to other viruses was unknown, but they said work on pathogens that could infect humans, animals or plants should not be pursued.

“Such genomes might encode new pathogens that … cannot be contained by existing countermeasures,” they wrote.

Tom Ellis, a professor of synthetic genome engineering at Imperial College London, said the work was impressive, but revealed how hard it would be to make more complex genomes. “This is literally the smallest and easiest genome to make,” he said.

An AI trained on the genetic code of dangerous bugs could be used to design more harmful viruses, Ellis said, but controlling access to genetic data and having restrictions on making genomes that look dangerous would help. “Governments are working hard to do this already,” he added.

“But honestly,” he said, “the threat from full AI design and writing of a genome of a virus or bacteria is very overblown when we consider that just taking existing pathogens and making gain-of-function changes to their genomes is so much easier and much more likely to be a real pathogenic threat.”

Dr Filippa Lentzos, a reader in science and international security at King’s College London, said the most important point to intervene at the moment was when DNA was being manufactured. “It’s important to see the bigger governance picture and not focus regulation solely on the AI model,” she said. “A layered approach makes more sense: safeguards around model development and access, responsible research review, synthesis screening, and established laboratory biosafety and biosecurity.”
